summary: AE/SE demo of hosted chat and text-generation basics focusing on streaming behavior, tuning parameters (temperature, max_tokens, top_p), and resilience patterns (retries, backoff, idempotency, fallbacks). Customer is interested in a 1-week pilot; security questions on SOC2, SSO, and data retention were raised.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Moreno: ok hi everyone thanks for joining from Redwood, I'm Alex, I'll run the demo and Priya is our SE. can you all hear me?
[00:05] Michael Torres: Yep, loud and clear.
[00:08] Sara Bennett: hi all
[00:12] Priya Shah: great, i'll share my screen in a sec, but quick agenda: hosted chat endpoint, params that matter for cost/latency, streaming behavior, and resilience patterns like retries and fallbacks. we'll leave time for security Qs at the end.
[00:26] Ravi Patel: sounds good — from SRE perspective our main asks are predictable p95 latency under load, and clear retry semantics for 429s.
[00:35] Alex Moreno: noted — we'll cover backoff recommendations and idempotency keys.
[00:40] [01:05] Priya Shah: ok sharing screen now, here's the Redwood Console quickstart page, and the Live Try-It — i'll start with a simple chat example. so the request body you care about is role/content pairs, plus generation params: max_tokens, temperature, top_p, n, stop. often customers ask which one to use — temperature controls randomness, top_p is nucleus sampling, we usually recommend temp 0.0-0.7 for product text.
[01:30] Michael Torres: can you show an example where streaming chunks arrive? how does that look over SSE vs websockets?
[01:36] Priya Shah: yeah — i'll switch to the API playground. when streaming is enabled you get incremental deltas. on SSE it's chunked events and the SDK surfaces token deltas, on websockets it's similar but persistent. here's a JS snippet we show in the docs: 
fetch(url, {method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify({model: 'redwood-small', messages: [...] , stream: true})})
.then(resp=>{ // resp.body is a readable stream 
 // read bytes and parse events 
})
[02:10] Sara Bennett: the console also shows token counts in the live trace?
[02:13] Priya Shah: yes, we show token-level cost estimates and a latency waterfall per request in the Console.
[02:20] [03:00] Alex Moreno: quick note on max_tokens — this caps generation length server-side and is the primary lever for unit cost. if you set max_tokens too high and expect short outputs you pay more on average. caching prefix or using few-shot prompts with short context helps.
[03:20] Michael Torres: do you support prefix caching or KV cache for conversational reuse?
[03:24] Priya Shah: yes, we have automatic prefix/KV caching for repeated contexts in Dedicated and Hosted; the runtime will reuse KV cache when it matches model variant and prompt prefix; there are caveats with prompt engineering and tokenization differences.
[03:40] Ravi Patel: about retries — suppose we see 429 or transient network errors, what's the recommended client behavior?
[03:46] Priya Shah: so first: treat 429 as rate-limited; implement exponential backoff with jitter. Redwood SDKs have a built-in retry module but if you're writing your own: start with base 200-300ms, double with cap around 2-5s, add full jitter. for idempotency on non-streaming generation use request-id header to dedupe; streaming calls are trickier because partial outputs may be emitted before failure. we recommend checkpointing or falling back to non-streaming single-response for critical flows.
[04:20] [04:50] Michael Torres: partial outputs — if the connection drops mid-stream, does Redwood buffer and let me reconnect?
[04:55] Priya Shah: currently we don't offer reconnect to resume mid-stream, but we provide event termination reasons and a final status so the client can be aware whether the model finished. for robust UX, we advise: small client-side timeouts, retry the whole request with the same prompt and idempotency key for non-critical multi-turns, or persist partial tokens if you need continuity.
[05:20] Sara Bennett: from a product POV we want deterministic summaries for customers, so bias towards lower temp is better?
[05:25] Priya Shah: yup, temp 0.0-0.3 for deterministic. also consider top_p tuning; lowering top_p provides a different control and sometimes reduces hallucination risk.
[05:40] [06:10] Alex Moreno: now i'll demo an example of retry behavior in our SDK — switching to the SE-run terminal. Priya: run the sample that simulates a 429 under load.
[06:20] Priya Shah: executing now — this script hits the endpoint at 100 RPS with backoff enabled; you'll see 429s and then exponential retries kick in, SDK captures and exposes metrics. (terminal noises) uh small typo in the script path, hold on.
[06:40] [07:05] Michael Torres: it's fine, scripted errors are expected. we want to know if retries cause duplicate charges.
[07:10] Priya Shah: good question — we guarantee at-least-once semantics for accepted tokens; for billing we charge for accepted completed calls. if retries cause the same request to be processed twice without idempotency, you can see double charges — that's why we suggest idempotency keys for non-streaming endpoints. for streaming, charge is on tokens emitted; if a retry replays and emits again you'll be billed twice for tokens.
[07:45] Ravi Patel: ok so use idempotency where possible and keep streaming for UX but be cautious about billing.
[07:52] Priya Shah: exactly.
[07:55] [08:30] Alex Moreno: another resilience pattern is model fallbacks — route to a smaller/faster model when latency SLOs are at risk, or return cached answer. Redwood can be configured in routing policies to prefer low-latency variants and fallback to cost variants.
[08:45] Michael Torres: can we do region failover? we're in GCP europe-west1.
[08:50] Priya Shah: yes, routing policies can select region-first or cost-first. Dedicated gives more control for pinned regions. for hosted we'll route to closest region by default but can be forced.
[09:10] [09:55] Sara Bennett: what about stop sequences — we have structured responses we want to parse reliably.
[09:59] Priya Shah: use explicit stop tokens, and consider streaming 'delta' parsing — you can parse JSON as it arrives but need to guard against partial JSON; Redwood supports structured output and function-calling primitives if you need schema guarantees.
[10:20] Alex Moreno: short break to go over security Qs — Jenna, can you remind us your top concerns?
[10:26] Jenna Cho: SOC2 evidence, SSO/SAML for console, audit logs at token/request level, and data residency. also interested in KMS integration for Private.
[10:35] Alex Moreno: we have SOC2 Type II summary and an SSO SAML guide, also audit logs export to your SIEM. i'll send the SOC2 excerpt now per next steps. Private supports customer-managed KMS.
[10:50] [11:20] Priya Shah: jumping back to the API: here's a typical curl example —
curl -X POST https://api.redwood.example/v1/chat/generate \n -H 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' \n -H 'Idempotency-Key: <uuid>' \n -d '{"model":"redwood-medium","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Summarize our meeting"}],"max_tokens":150,"temperature":0.2}'
[11:55] Michael Torres: nice. can you also show SDK behavior for streaming reconnection?
[11:59] Priya Shah: again, we don't support stream resume today, best is short streaming chunks and reconnection leads to re-request and possibly dedupe at app-level.
[12:20] [12:50] Alex Moreno: question from Danielle: are there built-in client-side examples for exponential backoff?
[12:55] Danielle Wu (Solutions): yes we include recommended backoff pseudocode and full JS/Go/Python wrappers that handle jitter and caps.
[13:05] Priya Shah: here's a link to the docs in the shared drive (posted in chat) — the sample shows start 300ms, multiply by 2, full jitter, cap 3s, max attempts 5.
[13:25] Michael Torres: what about concurrency limits at account level? if we go to 1k reqs/s will you throttle?
[13:30] Priya Shah: hosted has soft rate limits per API key that scale with usage; beyond that you'll see 429s. for predictable throughput we recommend Dedicated with reserved capacity. we can provide per-customer quotas for pilot.
[13:50] [14:40] Alex Moreno: switching to cost controls — Optimize can suggest quantization, batching, and model selection per workload; we can run a quick eval on your prompt set to show estimated unit cost difference between models.
[14:55] Sara Bennett: awesome — we'd love an eval comparing redwood-medium and redwood-small on our set.
[14:59] Priya Shah: we'll include that as part of the pilot.
[15:10] Michael Torres: about billing granularity — do we get per-route breakdown?
[15:14] Alex Moreno: yes Console has token-level cost breakdown per-route and per-model and you can export to CSV.
[15:25] [16:00] Ravi Patel: any guidance for long-running multi-turn sessions with KV cache expiry?
[16:05] Priya Shah: cache TTLs depend on model and variant; default is short-lived in hosted but you can configure in Dedicated. we'll capture session keys and reuse KV cache up to the TTL; also watch out for prompt drift and tokenization changes when upgrading models.
[16:32] [17:00] Priya Shah: quick live demo: I'll run a small script that streams a generated answer and intentionally kills the connection mid-way to simulate a drop. you'll see partial delta tokens in the logs and then a 499 or network error.
[17:20] (sound of keys)
[17:35] Michael Torres: yep saw it drop, the partial is visible in the Console trace.
[17:40] Priya Shah: right — for user-facing chat UX we recommend emitting partials to the UI and showing a reconnect button that triggers a safe re-request logic using idempotency keys or rehydration from last confirmed user turn.
[18:05] [18:50] Alex Moreno: wrapping up — recap of next steps and pilot plan. we'll send pricing and SOC2 now; Priya will own the benchmark script; schedule pilot kickoff for Apr 1, assume 1-week pilot, BlueLayer to provide prompt set and latency targets.
[19:10] Sara Bennett: sounds good. small Q — can we get a Dedicated sizing estimate if pilot looks promising?
[19:15] Alex Moreno: yes we'll include a Dedicated sizing worksheet and a cost/throughput worksheet.
[19:25] Michael Torres: final security question — retention: how long do you keep logs and are request payloads persisted?
[19:30] Alex Moreno: hosted retains logs for 30 days by default, audit exports available, and we can arrange extended retention for enterprise contracts. request payloads can be disabled for redaction; Private gives you full control.
[19:50] [20:30] Jenna Cho: noted — we'll review SOC2 and SSO guide.
[20:35] Alex Moreno: thanks everyone, recording and notes will be shared. we'll follow up with the links and action items.
[20:45] (call ends)
notes: Recording available in CRM and shared drive. Customer asked for a 1-week pilot starting Apr 1. Security artifacts and pricing to be sent. Heavy focus on streaming behavior and retries; recommended idempotency keys and exponential backoff with jitter.
